transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Blake (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Jordan, AE on the account, with Priya from our infra team. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Carlos Mendez (Verdant): Carlos here, head of platform. Aisha on security, Ethan our CTO joined as well. Sound check, yes.
[00:14] Priya Nair (Redwood SE): Hey all, Priya. We'll mostly listen then dig into networking questions.
[00:20] Ethan Liu (Verdant): Great. Our goal today is to understand what private deployment options look like and what the network/topology requirements are.
[00:27] Jordan: Awesome. Quick agenda: current infra, security constraints, VPC peering vs private endpoints, region considerations, and then next steps. Sound good?
[00:34] Aisha Khan (Verdant): Yep, especially interested in KMS, audit logs, and whether traffic leaves our VPC.
[00:40] Jordan: Totally. So quick background — Redwood supports Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. For Private (what you're exploring) we offer a customer-managed VPC deployment where the control plane sits in a private region or uses a customer VPC peering model, depending on needs.
[00:53] Carlos: When you say "control plane" — in private mode is there any component that sits in Redwood's shared plane or is it fully in our VPC?
[01:00] Priya: Good question. There are two common patterns we see: 1) VPC peering/direct connect style where our service endpoints live in a Redwood-managed VPC that you peer to or attach via TGW, and 2) private endpoints where we deploy a customer-dedicated control plane into your VPC (this latter is often used for stricter compliance). Both can be configured so inference workloads run in-region and data plane traffic does not traverse the public internet.
[01:22] Ethan: So for pattern 1, traffic crosses a peering connection into your VPC and stays there — but control signals might still go to Redwood?
[01:29] Priya: Right, with pattern 1 the management/control plane may be a Redwood-hosted endpoint in a private VPC in the same cloud region; the data plane — model inference — can be pinned to your dedicated hosts or remain in Redwood's dedicated hosts depending on contract. We can also flip to a fully customer-controlled deployment where everything lives within your VPC.
[01:47] Aisha: From security, we need to ensure logs, KMS keys, and SSO/SAML integration are under our control if possible. How do you manage KMS/HSM integration?
[01:56] Jordan: We support customer-managed keys via cloud KMS and HSM integrations. Priya?
[02:00] Priya: Yep. For private deployments we can integrate with your KMS (you provide key policies and grants). For on-prem or air-gapped we also support HSM integrations but the setup is more involved — we'll coordinate with your security and infra team on key exchange and least-privilege IAM roles.
[02:18] Carlos: Are audit logs pushed into our logging account or do you retain copies?
[02:23] Priya: We can forward audit logs to your logging destination — CloudWatch/Stackdriver/ELK — via a cross-account log sink. We also keep an internal audit trail for operations, but retention and export policies are configurable and part of the enterprise pack.
[02:35] Ethan: Region constraints: our workloads are in us-east-1 and europe-west-1. We need inference to be colocated with data in us-east-1 for latency. Do you host models in both?
[02:46] Jordan: We have infra in multiple regions — not every model type is available in every region. Priya can map which models and quantizations we can serve in us-east-1 with Dedicated/Private deployments.
[02:55] Priya: Correct. We maintain a catalog by region. For large LLMs we typically run them in certain preferred regions due to GPU availability. We can provide a recommended pairing for the models you intend to run; sometimes that means using a slightly smaller instance class to keep region parity.
[03:10] Aisha: Networking specifics — do you prefer VPC peering, PrivateLink/private endpoints, or Transit Gateway? We have a big TGW setup.
[03:19] Priya: Transit Gateway is actually our recommended pattern for customers with multiple VPCs or large enterprise topologies. It simplifies route management and supports scalable peering to Redwood-managed transit attachments. PrivateLink (interface endpoints) is also supported and is often used for strict IP allowlisting scenarios. VPC peering is simpler but can get messy at scale.
[03:38] Carlos: If we go TGW, is there a public IP egress to the internet for model downloads or updates?
[03:45] Priya: We can stage model artifacts in your S3 or in a shared, signed artifact store. Updates can be pulled over the peered connection; we don't require outbound internet egress from your VPC for normal operation. We do, however, need to coordinate control plane connectivity for management tasks unless we run a fully isolated control plane inside your VPC.
[04:03] Ethan: Can you describe what firewall rules and ports we need to open?
[04:07] Priya: For PrivateLink you'll open TCP 443 to the interface endpoints. For peering/TGW it's mostly TCP 443 plus a few gRPC ports if you use our low-latency streaming path — we'll provide a minimal list. Also SSH isn't required for normal operation; any admin access is via our control plane APIs and roles.
[04:25] Aisha: IP allowlist — do you provide static IPs for endpoints?
[04:29] Jordan: We can provide stable elastic IPs in some deployment patterns or you can use the private endpoints/PrivateLink model to avoid public IPs entirely. We'll outline both options.
[04:38] Carlos: What about cross-region replication or fallback — if us-east-1 has outage, can requests route to europe-west-1? Latency will suffer but availability matters.
[04:47] Priya: We have smart routing/fallbacks in the platform. For Private deployments, we can configure cross-region failover where model variants exist in both regions. If you need regional data residency guarantees, we can restrict failover. There's a tradeoff between availability and data sovereignty.
[05:03] Ethan: On the tenancy side — do you support dedicated GPU pools within our VPC or do you run on your hardware in our account?
[05:11] Priya: Two modes: 1) We deploy dedicated nodes into your VPC (we can run in your cloud account under a managed service principal) or 2) we keep hardware in Redwood-managed accounts and route traffic over TGW/peering. The former gives you maximum isolation; the latter is operationally simpler and faster to spin up.
[05:29] Aisha: For compliance we'd prefer the dedicated nodes in our account. How does billing work there?
[05:34] Jordan: We support a reserved capacity model for Dedicated/Private with monthly or annual commits. If instances live in your account, billing is invoiced based on reserved capacity and cloud usage; we can present a sample contract.
[05:44] Carlos: Any constraints on VPC CIDR ranges? We use /16s mostly.
[05:48] Priya: No hard constraint; we only ask for non-overlapping CIDRs with Redwood-managed VPCs. If there's overlap we need NAT or proxying which complicates routing. We'll need your exact ranges before the deep dive.
[05:59] Ethan: Latency — what's the expected p95 token latency if we run in-region Dedicated with 1k token sequences?
[06:07] Priya: Ballpark: for a medium-sized LLM in a dedicated, optimized runtime, p95 end-to-end might be 150-300ms per token depending on sequence length and batching. For large LLMs those numbers increase. We'll run benchmarks for your specific model set.
[06:22] Aisha: Benchmarking — can we run a POC that runs a fixed prompt set and you return both latency and token cost metrics?
[06:28] Jordan: Absolutely. Typical POCs include a workload runner and a synthetic prompt set. We can instrument cost, token counts, latency percentiles. Priya, what's needed from Verdant to run the POC?
[06:36] Priya: Your network ranges, a sample of prompts, model/size preferences, and whether you want the endpoint in your VPC or Redwood's dedicated VPC. Also credentials for any artifact buckets if you want model weights hosted in your account.
[06:47] Carlos: On auth and SSO — we use Okta SAML. You support SAML and RBAC?
[06:52] Jordan: Yes — SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning, plus RBAC at the team/route level. We'll include our SAML metadata in the pack.
[06:59] Aisha: Encryption at rest — is that enforced with our KMS?
[07:03] Priya: If you're on private deployment and you provide keys, yes. If you're on hosted we can also enable customer-managed keys for storage.
[07:10] Ethan: Data retention and logs — can you guarantee that raw request logs are not persisted outside of our retention window?
[07:16] Priya: Retention policies are configurable. By default we keep operation logs for 90 days, but for enterprise customers we can match your retention SLA and export logs to your account daily.
[07:26] Carlos: Any gotchas with IPv6? We haven't fully adopted it but wanted to know if you support it.
[07:31] Priya: IPv6 support is limited in some cloud provider networking constructs for PrivateLink; best practice is to use IPv4 for our private endpoints today. We can revisit if you need dual-stack.
[07:41] Jordan: Quick pause — seems like agreement that next is a deep technical session. Any blockers or red flags from Verdant side?
[07:47] Carlos: Mostly need to validate model availability in us-east-1 and the cost implications of dedicated nodes in our account. Also need security pack.
[07:55] Aisha: And we need details on KMS integrations and exact audit log export steps.
[08:00] Priya: We'll prepare a doc that maps models to regions, expected throughput per instance type, and sample routing diagrams for TGW vs PrivateLink vs peering.
[08:10] Ethan: Regarding model updates — if Redwood pushes a model update, can we control the rollout? Canary?
[08:16] Jordan: Yes, our Rollouts feature supports canary deploys, A/B tests, and automatic fallback. You can pin versions or let the platform manage gradual rollouts.
[08:25] Carlos: One final question — what's the usual lead time to get a private deployment up and running?
[08:30] Priya: For the simplest peering-based private deployment, we can stand up infra in 2-4 weeks once networking and IAM are agreed. For fully customer-account-dedicated nodes it's typically 4-8 weeks because of account setup and security reviews.
[08:44] Aisha: That's reasonable. We'll want a checklist for security review.
[08:48] Jordan: We'll attach our compliance checklist with the security pack.
[08:51] [longer discussion about pricing & contract models omitted for brevity]
[37:10] Priya: (picking back up) A few more nitty-gritty: for model artifact storage we recommend using signed S3 buckets with least-privilege roles. We can stage artifacts in your bucket using role grants. That avoids public artifact pulls.
[37:23] Carlos: Good. Regarding network monitoring — do you emit metrics into our Prometheus or do you expose an endpoint?
[37:29] Priya: We can emit metrics to your observability stack via a metrics forwarder or push to a managed endpoint. We also offer per-route dashboards in the Redwood Console.
[37:38] Ethan: For the POC let's target one model family, run 5k requests with your standard prompt set, and capture p50/p95/p99.
[37:45] Jordan: Sounds good. We'll draft the POC scope in the next 48 hours.
[37:50] Aisha: Any network changes required on our side for PrivateLink?
[37:54] Priya: You'll need to create interface endpoints and security groups allowing the Redwood operational CIDRs. We'll send a template SG and endpoint creation steps.
[38:03] Carlos: Ok. We'll get the CIDRs and TGW topology to you.
[38:07] Jordan: Perfect. Recap of next steps: I'll send security pack and sample peering diagram by Monday (2026-04-12). Priya will schedule tech deep dive week of 4/20 and prepare model-to-region mapping. Carlos will share CIDRs and TGW details. Anything else?
[38:22] Ethan: Please include estimated cost ranges for dedicated nodes vs using Redwood-managed hosts.
[38:27] Jordan: Will do.
[38:29] Aisha: Thanks everyone.
[38:31] Jordan: Thanks all — we'll follow up with calendar invites.
[38:34] [End of meeting]

Notes: transcript includes some minor transcription artifacts; some brand names may be slightly garbled. References to PrivateLink/VPC/TGW are accurate for context.
